messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Rangi is a 63-year-old Māori man, widowed, who has worked in construction for the better part of four decades. He came to his first intake appointment with the quiet, careful bearing of someone who has spent a long time trying to take up as little space as possible — a quality that sits strangely against his large frame and weathered hands. His PCL-5 score of 68 places him in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first few sessions was one of a man whose interior life had been quietly dismantled over years of abuse by his late wife, and who had only recently begun to understand that what happened to him had a name.

The abuse began gradually, as it so often does, and escalated over more than a decade. His wife's attacks were physical — striking, grabbing, once fracturing two of his fingers when she slammed a door on his hand during an argument. What Rangi remembers most vividly is the specific geography of those moments: her hands around his wrist, the particular angle of an arm raised, the sight of bruising on his own forearms in the bathroom mirror the following morning. He never called the police. He told no one. He was, he believed, supposed to be able to handle it.

She died of a cardiac event three years ago, and it was in the silence that followed that the symptoms arrived in full. Now, at work on a construction site, Rangi finds that certain visual details carry an almost physical charge. A co-worker's forearm raised to wipe sweat from a brow, a supervisor gesturing sharply during a briefing, even the sight of his own hands at the end of a shift — these images land with a force disproportionate to their content, pulling him back into the sensory texture of the abuse. When the crew talks at lunch and someone mentions a domestic dispute they heard about on the news, Rangi goes quiet and finds a reason to leave the table. People who knew him and his wife — a brother-in-law who still calls occasionally, a neighbour from the old street — have become almost impossible to be around; their presence makes the past feel present in a way he cannot manage.

When these triggers catch him off-guard, Rangi's first instinct is to move. He has made a habit of positioning himself near doors — on the site, in the canteen, in any room he enters — scanning for exits the moment he walks in, a behaviour so automatic now he barely notices it until a colleague comments on it. He also spends money in ways he cannot always account for: tools he doesn't need, takeaway meals, a new television he barely watches. He understands, dimly, that he is trying to fill something or outrun something, but the spending brings a few hours of relief before the flatness returns. And he avoids conflict with a rigidity that has begun to cost him professionally — he has declined to raise legitimate safety concerns on site, has let errors go unchallenged, has been passed over for a foreman role he was qualified for because, as his site manager noted, he "doesn't push back."

The avoidance has fed something darker. Because Rangi never talks about what happened, never allows himself to be around those connected to it, the events remain unprocessed and close to the surface — and the triggers, when they come, feel as raw as ever. He wakes in the night, alert and listening, certain for a moment that he is not safe, and lies still until he has checked the room. He startles at sounds on the site — a dropped beam, a shout across the yard — in ways that embarrass him deeply. And that embarrassment compounds what has become his most corrosive belief: that he is weak. A real man, he tells himself, would not have let this happen, and would not still be undone by it. He cannot rely on himself to stay steady, to react normally, to be the person he was before. He feels, much of the time, dead inside — not grief exactly, but an absence where feeling used to be.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was his youngest daughter, who visited recently and told him, plainly, that she was frightened for him. He sat with that for two weeks before making the call. What he is most afraid of, he said at the end of the first session, is that the man he used to be is simply gone. What he hopes, more quietly, is that someone might tell him he is wrong.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat directly drives or leads to his maladaptive strategies (e.g., exit-scanning, avoidance, spending); the strategies are linked to triggers catching him off-guard, not to an ongoing perceived threat.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat causes or activates his triggers; the vignette describes triggers arising from environmental cues at work and social situations, but does not establish that a felt sense of threat produces or amplifies those triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She died of a cardiac event three years ago, and it was in the silence that followed that the symptoms arrived in full. Now, at work on a construction site, Rangi finds that certain visual details carry an almost physical charge.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
What he carries onto the site each morning is not merely memory but a persistent, bodily sense that danger has not passed — that the world remains the kind of place where harm comes from the people closest to you. Living at that pitch of alertness, he finds the site dense with signals his nervous system cannot stop reading: a raised forearm, a sharp gesture, his own bruised knuckles after a hard day's work all arrive already charged, because his body has decided, before any of it happens, that threat is present.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When these triggers catch him off-guard, Rangi's first instinct is to move.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But it is not only the triggers themselves that drive this — it is the unrelenting sense of threat that underlies every hour of his day. When the world feels that dangerous, positioning himself near exits and scanning every room he enters is not a symptom he can name; it is simply what a person does to stay safe. The spending, the conflict avoidance, the careful management of who he is around — all of it flows from the same source: a felt conviction that he cannot afford to be caught off-guard again.
<<<END>>>
